os-fundamentals-001.title: Print Working Directory
os-fundamentals-001.instructions: Write the command to print your current working directory.
os-fundamentals-001.explanation: `pwd` prints the path of the current working directory.

os-fundamentals-002.title: Identify Current User
os-fundamentals-002.instructions: Write the command that displays the effective username of the current shell session.
os-fundamentals-002.explanation: `whoami` prints the effective username for the current shell session.

os-fundamentals-003.title: Show Date and Time
os-fundamentals-003.instructions: Write the command to display the current date and time.
os-fundamentals-003.explanation: `date` displays the system date and time.

os-fundamentals-004.title: View Command History
os-fundamentals-004.instructions: Write the command to show a numbered list of previously executed commands.

os-fundamentals-005.title: Manual Page Access
os-fundamentals-005.instructions: Write the command to open the manual page for the `ls` command.
hints: Use `man` followed by the command name.

os-fundamentals-006.title: Absolute Path Concept
os-fundamentals-006.instructions: What type of path starts explicitly with the root slash `/`?
hints: It gives the full path from root.
os-fundamentals-006.explanation: An absolute path starts from the root directory `/`.

os-fundamentals-007.title: Inode Metadata
os-fundamentals-007.instructions: Write the command to show a long directory listing with each entry’s inode number.
os-fundamentals-007.explanation: `ls -li` combines the long listing with inode-number output.

os-fundamentals-008.title: Parent Directory Reference
os-fundamentals-008.instructions: In relative pathing, what symbol represents the parent directory?

os-fundamentals-009.title: Current Directory Reference
os-fundamentals-009.instructions: What symbol represents the current directory in relative paths?

os-fundamentals-010.title: List Inode Numbers Explicitly
os-fundamentals-010.instructions: Write the command to list file names with their inode numbers in long format.
os-fundamentals-010.explanation: `ls -li` combines long listing with inode numbers.

os-fundamentals-011.title: Display Current User ID
os-fundamentals-011.instructions: Write the command to print your user ID and group IDs.

os-shell-basics-012.title: Combine Short Options
os-shell-basics-012.instructions: Write a command to list all files (including hidden ones) in long format for the `/etc` directory by combining `-l` and `-a` into a single combined option string.
hints: Combine flags after a single dash.
os-shell-basics-012.explanation: Short options can be combined after a single dash like `-la`.

os-shell-basics-013.title: Repeat Last Command
os-shell-basics-013.instructions: Write the shell shorthand symbol used to repeat the immediately preceding command.

os-shell-basics-015.title: Command Separator
os-shell-basics-015.instructions: Write a single-line command sequence using a semicolon to change directory to `/tmp` and then list its contents.
os-shell-basics-015.explanation: Semicolon `;` runs multiple commands sequentially on one line.

os-shell-basics-016.title: Brace Expansion Creation
os-shell-basics-016.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression with `touch` to create three files named `log1.txt`, `log2.txt`, and `log3.txt` in one command.
os-shell-basics-016.explanation: Brace expansion `{1..3}` generates sequential strings `log1.txt log2.txt log3.txt`.

os-shell-basics-017.title: Directory Tree Brace Expansion
os-shell-basics-017.instructions: Write a command using `mkdir -p` and brace expansion to create a directory structure `project/src`, `project/docs`, and `project/tests` all at once.
os-shell-basics-017.explanation: `mkdir -p project/{src,docs,tests}` creates the base directory and three subdirectories simultaneously.

os-shell-basics-020.title: Exit Shell
os-shell-basics-020.instructions: Write the command or shortcut key sequence to exit the current shell session.
os-shell-basics-020.explanation: Typing `exit` or pressing `Ctrl+D` exits the shell.

os-shell-basics-021.title: Execute a Numbered History Entry
os-shell-basics-021.instructions: In Bash, write the history expansion that reruns command number 3 from the current history list.
hints: Exclamation mark followed by the number.
os-shell-basics-021.explanation: `!3` expands to and executes the command with history number 3.

os-shell-basics-022.title: Echo Variable
os-shell-basics-022.instructions: Write an `echo` command to print the value of a shell variable `USER`.

os-shell-basics-023.title: Long Options Prefix
os-shell-basics-023.instructions: Write the standard prefix formatting (number of dashes) for long options in Linux commands.
os-shell-basics-023.explanation: Long option names start with two dashes (`--`).

os-shell-basics-025.title: Brace Expansion Letters
os-shell-basics-025.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to echo letters `a`, `b`, and `c` separated by spaces.
os-shell-basics-025.explanation: `echo {a..c}` prints `a b c` via brace expansion.

os-wildcards-027.title: Match Any Characters
os-wildcards-027.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match any filename ending in `.txt`.
hints: Use `*` for any number of characters.
os-wildcards-027.explanation: `*` matches any number of characters, including none.

os-wildcards-028.title: Match Single Character
os-wildcards-028.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match `file1.txt`, `file2.txt`, etc., where exactly one single character replaces the question mark in `file?.txt`.

os-wildcards-029.title: Character List Bracket
os-wildcards-029.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern using brackets to match files starting with `a`, `b`, or `c` followed by anything.
os-wildcards-029.explanation: `[abc]*` matches names starting with `a`, `b`, or `c` followed by any characters.

os-wildcards-030.title: Negated Bracket Wildcard
os-wildcards-030.instructions: Write a Bash filename-glob pattern that matches names whose first character is not a digit from 0 through 9.
hints: Use `!` or `^` inside brackets for negation.
os-wildcards-030.explanation: In Bash filename globbing, `[!0-9]` matches one character outside the digit range; the trailing `*` matches the rest of the name.

os-wildcards-031.title: Digit Range Wildcard
os-wildcards-031.instructions: Write a Bash filename-glob pattern that matches a name beginning with `log`, followed by exactly one digit, followed by `.txt`.
os-wildcards-031.explanation: `[0-9]` matches exactly one digit in a Bash filename glob.

os-wildcards-032.title: Hidden Files Globbing
os-wildcards-032.instructions: True or False: Standard wildcards like `*` match leading dots, so they automatically match hidden files without explicit notation.
hints: Hidden files start with a dot '.' which is ignored by standard `*`.
os-wildcards-032.explanation: `*` and `?` do not match a leading dot; hidden files require explicit dot notation.

os-wildcards-034.title: Letter Range Brace Expansion
os-wildcards-034.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to generate letters `a` through `c`.

os-wildcards-035.title: Comma Brace Expansion
os-wildcards-035.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to generate `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`.

os-wildcards-036.title: List Log Files Glob
os-wildcards-036.instructions: Write a `ls` command using a wildcard to list all `.log` files in the current directory.

os-wildcards-037.title: Match Specific Range
os-wildcards-037.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern matching any single lowercase letter from `a` to `z` followed by `.txt`.
os-wildcards-037.explanation: `[a-z].txt` matches a single lowercase letter filename ending in `.txt`.

os-wildcards-039.title: List Files Starting with Letter
os-wildcards-039.instructions: Write an `ls` command using a wildcard to list files starting with `a`.

os-wildcards-040.title: List Single Character Extension
os-wildcards-040.instructions: Write an `ls` command using `?` to list files named `fileX.txt` where `X` is any single character.
os-wildcards-040.explanation: `ls file?.txt` matches a single character position.

os-wildcards-041.title: Match Zero or More
os-wildcards-041.instructions: Which wildcard symbol matches any number of characters, including zero characters?

os-navigation-042.title: Change Directory Home
os-navigation-042.instructions: Write the command to change your current directory to your home directory.
os-navigation-042.explanation: `cd` or `cd ~` navigates to the user's home directory.

os-navigation-043.title: Go Back Previous Directory
os-navigation-043.instructions: Write the command to return to the previous directory you were in.
os-navigation-043.explanation: `cd -` switches back to the previous working directory.

os-navigation-044.title: Go Up Parent Directory
os-navigation-044.instructions: Write the command to move up one directory level.

os-navigation-045.title: List Long Format
os-navigation-045.instructions: Write the `ls` command to list directory contents in long format.
os-navigation-045.explanation: `ls -l` shows permissions, link counts, owners, sizes, and timestamps.

os-navigation-046.title: List Hidden Files
os-navigation-046.instructions: Write the `ls` command that lists all entries, including hidden entries and the special `.` and `..` entries.
os-navigation-046.explanation: `ls -a` includes hidden names as well as `.` and `..`.

os-navigation-047.title: List Directory Itself
os-navigation-047.instructions: Write the command to list the attributes and details of the `/etc` directory itself rather than its contents.
os-navigation-047.explanation: `ls -d` lists the directory itself rather than its contents.

os-navigation-048.title: Recursive Listing
os-navigation-048.instructions: Write the `ls` option that recursively lists all contents of subdirectories.

os-navigation-049.title: Human Readable Sizes
os-navigation-049.instructions: Which `ls` option displays file sizes in a human-readable form such as KiB or MiB when used with a long listing?
os-navigation-049.explanation: `-h` makes sizes human-readable; it is commonly combined with `-l`.

os-navigation-051.title: Print Date Format
os-navigation-051.instructions: Write the `date` command option to format output as `YYYY-MM-DD` (using `%F`).
os-navigation-051.explanation: `date +%F` prints the date in ISO format (`YYYY-MM-DD`).

os-navigation-052.title: Quit Manual Page
os-navigation-052.instructions: What key do you press to quit out of a `man` manual page view?

os-navigation-053.title: Search in Man Page
os-navigation-053.instructions: Which symbol/character do you type inside `man` to start searching for text?
os-navigation-053.explanation: Typing `/` followed by search terms allows searching inside `man` and `less`.

os-navigation-054.title: Root Directory Path
os-navigation-054.instructions: Write the command to change your directory to the topmost root directory `/`.

os-navigation-055.title: Combined Listing Options
os-navigation-055.instructions: Write an `ls` command that combines long format, hidden files, and human-readable sizes.
os-navigation-055.explanation: `ls -lah` combines long format, all hidden files, and human-readable sizes.

os-navigation-056.title: List One Per Line
os-navigation-056.instructions: Write the `ls` option to output exactly one entry per line.

os-navigation-059.title: Navigation MCQ Concept
os-navigation-059.instructions: Which command prints the absolute path of the current working directory?
os-navigation-059.explanation: `pwd` prints the full path of the current directory.

os-file-inspection-062.title: Check File Type

os-file-inspection-062.explanation: `file` reports the classification and type of a file.

os-file-inspection-063.title: View Metadata Stat
os-file-inspection-063.instructions: Write the command to display detailed metadata (size, inode, permissions, timestamps) for `notes.txt`.
os-file-inspection-063.explanation: `stat` displays detailed low-level file metadata and timestamps.

os-file-inspection-064.title: Print Entire File
os-file-inspection-064.instructions: Write the command to print the entire contents of `notes.txt` to the terminal screen.
os-file-inspection-064.explanation: `cat` outputs the complete contents of files.

os-file-inspection-065.title: View First Lines
os-file-inspection-065.instructions: Write the command to display the first 5 lines of `notes.txt`.
os-file-inspection-065.explanation: `head -n 5` prints the first 5 lines of a file.

os-file-inspection-066.title: View Last Lines
os-file-inspection-066.instructions: Write the command to display the last 20 lines of `logfile.txt`.
os-file-inspection-066.explanation: `tail -n 20` prints the final 20 lines of a file.

os-file-inspection-067.title: Follow Log File
os-file-inspection-067.instructions: Write the `tail` command option that continuously follows and outputs new lines appended to a growing log file.
os-file-inspection-067.explanation: `tail -f` keeps the stream open and outputs new lines as they are appended.

os-file-inspection-068.title: Page by Page Viewer
os-file-inspection-068.instructions: Write the command to inspect a large file page by page with bi-directional scrolling and search capability.
os-file-inspection-068.explanation: `less` is a pager allowing backward and forward navigation through files.

os-file-inspection-069.title: Count Lines Words Bytes
os-file-inspection-069.instructions: Write the command to count the number of lines, words, and bytes in `notes.txt`.
os-file-inspection-069.explanation: `wc` reports newline, word, and byte counts.

os-file-inspection-072.title: Join Multiple Files
os-file-inspection-072.instructions: Write a `cat` command that combines and prints the contents of `a.txt` and `b.txt` together.
os-file-inspection-072.explanation: `cat` can concatenate and print multiple files sequentially.

os-file-inspection-073.title: Head First Ten
os-file-inspection-073.instructions: Write a `head` command to print the first 10 lines of `data.txt` explicitly.
os-file-inspection-073.explanation: `head` prints the first lines of files.

os-file-inspection-074.title: Quit Less Pager
os-file-inspection-074.instructions: Write the key pressed inside `less` or `man` to quit the view.

os-file-inspection-075.title: Tail Last Ten
os-file-inspection-075.instructions: Write a `tail` command to print the last 10 lines of `data.txt` explicitly.
os-file-inspection-075.explanation: `tail` prints the final lines of files.

os-file-inspection-076.title: Command Comparison
os-file-inspection-076.instructions: Which inspection command allows scrolling both forward and backward through a file?
hints: Name implies it's more versatile than `more`.
os-file-inspection-076.explanation: `less` allows bidirectional navigation whereas `more` is mainly forward-only.

os-file-management-077.title: Create Directory

os-file-management-078.title: Create Parent Directories

os-file-management-079.title: Create Empty File

os-file-management-084.title: Interactive Move Prompt

os-file-management-085.title: Remove File

os-file-management-090.title: Move into Directory
os-file-management-090.instructions: Write a `mv` command to move `report.txt` into the `docs/` directory.
os-file-management-090.explanation: `mv` moves the file into the target directory.

os-file-management-091.title: Recycle Bin Warning
os-file-management-091.instructions: True or False: Linux command-line deletion via `rm` moves deleted files to a temporary desktop recycle bin.
os-file-management-091.explanation: Linux command-line `rm` permanently unlinks files; there is no recycle bin.

os-file-management-092.title: Create Multiple Empty
os-file-management-092.instructions: Write a `touch` command to create two empty files `one.txt` and `two.txt` simultaneously.
os-file-management-092.explanation: `touch` accepts multiple filenames to create or update them.

os-file-management-093.title: Nested Mkdir
os-file-management-093.instructions: Write a `mkdir` command to create `project/src/core` in a single command.

os-file-management-095.title: Interactive Rm

os-text-utilities-099.title: Cut Fields Column
os-text-utilities-099.instructions: Write a `cut` command to extract the first column/field from `/etc/passwd` using `:` as the delimiter.

os-text-utilities-100.title: Sort Numerically
os-text-utilities-100.instructions: Write the `sort` command option to sort numbers in numerical order rather than alphabetical order.

os-text-utilities-102.title: Uniq Count Occurrences
os-text-utilities-102.instructions: Write the `uniq` command option to prefix each unique line with its count of occurrences.

os-text-utilities-103.title: Uniq Duplicate Lines

os-text-utilities-104.title: Tr Translate Lower Upper

os-text-utilities-107.title: Tee Append Option

os-text-utilities-109.title: Process Status Ps

os-redirection-122.explanation: `<` redirects a file into standard input of a command.

os-redirection-123.title: Pipe Connector

os-networking-278.explanation: An IPv4 address consists of four decimal octets, each in the range 0–255.

os-networking-279.title: IPv6 Address Structure
os-networking-279.instructions: An address contains hexadecimal groups separated by colons, such as `2001:0db8:...`. Which protocol version is it?
hints: It is the newer IP addressing format.
os-networking-279.explanation: IPv6 addresses use hexadecimal groups separated by colons.

os-networking-280.title: Loopback Address
os-networking-280.instructions: A service running on your own machine must be reached through the local host interface. Which IPv4 address is the loopback address?
hints: It is the familiar address in the 127.0.0.0 range.
os-networking-280.explanation: `127.0.0.1` is the IPv4 loopback address and refers to the same computer.

os-networking-281.title: DNS Purpose
os-networking-281.instructions: You enter `www.kdg.be` in a browser. What does DNS provide before the browser connects to the server?
options: A translation from the hostname to an IP address
A list of local file permissions
A compressed copy of the website
hints: DNS acts like a directory for network names.
os-networking-281.explanation: A Domain Name System server translates a domain name into an IP address.

os-networking-282.title: HTTP and HTTPS Ports
os-networking-282.instructions: A web server offers ordinary HTTP and HTTPS. Which pair of default ports is used in that order?
hints: The encrypted web service uses the higher of these two familiar ports.
os-networking-282.explanation: The course identifies port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS.

os-networking-283.title: SSH Default Port
os-networking-283.instructions: A remote Linux server accepts SSH connections using the standard port. Which port should the client normally reach?
hints: It is the standard Secure Shell port.
os-networking-283.explanation: SSH services normally listen on TCP port 22.

os-networking-284.title: Find Linux Interface Addresses
os-networking-284.instructions: Write the Linux command used to display network interfaces and their IP addresses.
hints: It begins with the two-letter network utility.
os-networking-284.explanation: `ip a` displays network interfaces and their addresses; the address is shown on an `inet` line.

os-networking-285.title: SSH Remote Login
os-networking-285.instructions: You have the username `student` and the remote server address `server.example`. Write the command to open a remote text-shell session.
hints: Use the secure shell client with `user@host`.
os-networking-285.explanation: `ssh user@address` opens a secure remote shell session when the server provides the SSH service.

os-networking-286.title: SSH Host Fingerprint
os-networking-286.instructions: During the first SSH connection, the client asks you to confirm a host key fingerprint. What is the main purpose of checking it?
options: To verify the identity of the remote server
To choose the user’s primary group
To set the SSH port to 80
To create a new home directory
hints: It helps you detect that you are connecting to the intended host.
os-networking-286.explanation: The host key fingerprint helps verify the remote server’s identity before trusting the connection.

os-directories-287.title: Administrative Binary Directory
os-directories-287.instructions: Where are many system-administration executable commands located in the standard filesystem hierarchy?
hints: It is the sibling directory of `/usr/bin`.
os-directories-287.explanation: `/usr/sbin` contains many administrative binaries, while `/usr/bin` contains ordinary user commands.

os-directories-288.title: Variable Data Directory
os-directories-288.instructions: A service stores changing data such as logs, mail queues, or databases. Which top-level directory is intended for this kind of data?
hints: The directory name relates to variable data.
os-directories-288.explanation: `/var` stores variable data; system log files are commonly under `/var/log`.

os-directories-289.title: Filesystem Case Sensitivity
os-directories-289.instructions: A script refers to `/etc/Passwd`, but the actual file is `/etc/passwd`. What should you expect on a case-sensitive Linux filesystem?
options: Both names refer to the same file
They are different names, so the first path may not exist
Linux converts both paths to lowercase
The shell searches all files for a similar name
hints: Uppercase and lowercase letters are not interchangeable in Linux filenames.
os-directories-289.explanation: Linux paths are case-sensitive: `/etc/Passwd` and `/etc/passwd` are different names.

os-navigation-290.title: Home Directory of Another User
os-navigation-290.instructions: Write a Bash path expression that refers to the home directory of user `alice`.
hints: Use tilde expansion followed immediately by the username.
os-navigation-290.explanation: `~alice` expands to the home directory of user `alice`.

os-navigation-291.title: Trailing Slash in a Path
os-navigation-291.instructions: What does a trailing slash in `/var/log/` communicate about the path?
options: The path must refer to a directory
The path must refer to an executable file
The path is relative to the current directory
The final component is a symbolic link
hints: The slash marks the path as a directory path.
os-navigation-291.explanation: A trailing slash indicates that the path is expected to be a directory.

os-navigation-292.title: Relative Path Depends on CWD
os-navigation-292.instructions: You are in `/home/alice/docs`. What absolute path does `../notes.txt` refer to?
os-navigation-292.explanation: `..` moves from `/home/alice/docs` to `/home/alice`, so the resolved path is `/home/alice/notes.txt`.

os-file-inspection-293.title: File Type Does Not Depend on Extension
os-file-inspection-293.instructions: A file is named `report.txt`, but its contents are a PNG image. Which command helps identify its actual file type?
hints: Use the command that inspects file content rather than relying on its suffix.
os-file-inspection-293.explanation: The `file` command identifies a file type from its contents; Linux does not determine type solely from the filename extension.

os-file-inspection-294.title: Access Modify Change Birth Times
os-file-inspection-294.instructions: Which command displays file timestamps including access, modification, status change, and birth information?
hints: It reports detailed metadata for a filesystem object.
os-file-inspection-294.explanation: `stat` displays metadata such as size, inode, permissions, and timestamps.

os-file-inspection-295.title: Longest Line Length
os-file-inspection-295.instructions: Write a command to display the length of the longest line in `notes.txt`.
hints: Use the line-length option of the word-count utility.
os-file-inspection-295.explanation: `wc -L` reports the length of the longest line in the input file.

os-file-inspection-296.title: Numbered File Output
os-file-inspection-296.instructions: Write a command to display `/etc/passwd` with line numbers.
hints: The exercise uses the numbering option of `cat`.

os-file-inspection-297.title: Tail From a Specific Line
os-file-inspection-297.instructions: Write a command that displays `/etc/passwd` starting at line 30 and continues through the end of the file.
hints: For `tail -n`, a plus sign means start at the specified line.

os-text-utilities-298.title: Number Lines in a Stream
os-text-utilities-298.instructions: Write a command that numbers each line arriving on standard input.
hints: The utility’s name is short for numbering lines.
os-text-utilities-298.explanation: `nl` adds line numbers to input lines.

os-text-utilities-299.title: Compare Two Text Files
os-text-utilities-299.instructions: Two files should contain identical text, but you need to see their differences. Which command compares them?
hints: Use the comparison utility named in the capstone exercise.
os-text-utilities-299.explanation: `diff` compares two files and reports differences; no output indicates no differences.

os-text-utilities-300.title: Sort by a Specific Field
os-text-utilities-300.instructions: Write a `sort` command that sorts `records.txt` using the second whitespace-delimited field as the sort key.
os-text-utilities-300.explanation: `sort -k 2` uses the second field as the sort key.

os-text-utilities-301.title: Case-Insensitive Sorting
os-text-utilities-301.instructions: Which `sort` option makes sorting ignore differences between uppercase and lowercase letters?

os-text-utilities-302.title: Transform Standard Input
os-text-utilities-302.instructions: Why does `tr` normally appear with a pipe or input redirection when processing a file?
options: It reads from standard input and writes to standard output
It edits a file in place by default
It requires an archive as input
hints: Think about where the utility receives its input stream.
os-text-utilities-302.explanation: `tr` reads from standard input and writes transformed text to standard output.

os-text-utilities-303.title: Echo Without a Trailing Newline
os-text-utilities-303.instructions: Write an `echo` command to print `Ready` without adding a newline at the end.
hints: Use the no-newline option shown in the command-line exercises.
os-text-utilities-303.explanation: `echo -n` prints the text without the usual trailing newline.

os-text-utilities-304.title: Extract Two Fields
os-text-utilities-304.instructions: Write a command to extract fields 1 and 5 from `/etc/passwd`, using the colon as the delimiter.
hints: Set the delimiter with `-d` and the selected fields with `-f`.
os-text-utilities-304.explanation: `cut -d ':' -f 1,5` extracts the first and fifth colon-separated fields.

os-text-utilities-305.title: Unique Lines in a Pipeline
os-text-utilities-305.instructions: A file contains repeated animal names on separate lines. Write a pipeline that sorts the names and then removes adjacent duplicates.
os-text-utilities-305.explanation: Sorting first groups equal lines together; `uniq` then removes the adjacent duplicates.

os-text-utilities-306.title: Save and Display a Process List
os-text-utilities-306.instructions: Write a pipeline that displays all running processes, saves the same output in `processes.txt`, and leaves the stream available to continue through the pipe.
hints: Use the command that duplicates a stream to a file and standard output.
os-text-utilities-306.explanation: `tee` writes a copy to the file and sends the stream onward (and to the terminal when not piped further).

os-text-utilities-307.title: Pipe Data into a Pager
os-text-utilities-307.instructions: Write a pipeline to display a long listing of `/usr/bin` one screen at a time.
hints: The second command should be the bidirectional pager.
os-text-utilities-307.explanation: The pipe sends the listing to `less`, allowing screen-by-screen navigation.

os-text-utilities-308.title: Count Running Processes
os-text-utilities-308.instructions: Write a command pipeline that counts the lines in the full process listing produced by `ps aux`.
hints: Count the lines in the process-listing stream.
os-text-utilities-308.explanation: `ps aux` generates the listing and `wc -l` counts its lines.

os-help-309.title: Quick Help for an Executable
os-help-309.instructions: You know a command name but need a short summary of its options without opening a manual page. What should you append to the command?
hints: It is the standard long option for a brief help summary.
os-help-309.explanation: Many executable commands support `--help` to display a concise option summary.

os-help-310.title: Help for a Shell Built-in
os-help-310.instructions: Write the Bash command that displays built-in help for `cd`.
hints: Use the shell’s built-in help command.
os-help-310.explanation: `help cd` displays help for the Bash built-in command `cd`.

os-help-311.title: Identify a Built-in or Executable
os-help-311.instructions: Write a command that determines whether `cd` is a shell built-in or an external executable.
os-help-311.explanation: `type cd` reports that `cd` is a shell built-in.

os-help-312.title: Manual Page for a File Format
os-help-312.instructions: You need documentation for the format of `/etc/passwd`, not the interactive password-changing command. Which manual page should you open?
hints: File formats are documented in manual section 5.
os-help-312.explanation: `man 5 passwd` opens the manual page describing the passwd file format; section 1 covers user commands.

os-help-313.title: Search Manual Page Descriptions
os-help-313.instructions: You have forgotten the command name for changing file permissions. Which command searches manual-page names and short descriptions for the keyword `permission`?
hints: This is a keyword search of the manual-page index.
os-help-313.explanation: `man -k` and `apropos` search manual-page names and short descriptions.

os-help-314.title: Manual Sections for Commands
os-help-314.instructions: Which manual section normally describes commands that users can run from the shell?
hints: The first section is for user commands.
os-help-314.explanation: Manual section 1 documents user commands; section 5 documents file formats.

os-help-315.title: Package Documentation Directory
os-help-315.instructions: A package installs README files, examples, and sample configuration files. Which standard directory should you inspect for this documentation?
hints: It is the shared documentation directory.
os-help-315.explanation: Package documentation is commonly installed under `/usr/share/doc/<package>-<version>/`.

os-help-316.title: Optional Notation in a Synopsis
os-help-316.instructions: In a manual-page synopsis, what do square brackets around an option or argument normally indicate?
options: The item must be typed literally
The item is a filename extension
hints: Brackets show whether a part can be omitted.
os-help-316.explanation: Square brackets in a command synopsis indicate optional syntax.

os-help-317.title: Navigate Info Documentation
os-help-317.instructions: Which key quits the interactive `pinfo` reader?
hints: It is the same single-letter quit key used in several terminal pagers.

os-users-groups-318.title: Read the Seven Passwd Fields
os-users-groups-318.instructions: In an `/etc/passwd` record, which field contains the user’s login shell?
hints: The shell is the final field in the seven-field record.
os-users-groups-318.explanation: The seven fields are username, password placeholder, UID, primary GID, comment, home directory, and login shell.

os-users-groups-319.title: Passwd Password Placeholder
os-users-groups-319.instructions: An `/etc/passwd` line contains `x` in its second field. What does that indicate?
options: The password hash is stored in `/etc/shadow`
The user’s primary group is disabled
The account is a system service
hints: The actual password hash is stored in a more restricted file.
os-users-groups-319.explanation: The `x` placeholder indicates that password information is stored in `/etc/shadow`.

os-users-groups-320.title: Group Record Fields
os-users-groups-320.instructions: What does the fourth colon-separated field in `/etc/group` contain?
options: A comma-separated list of supplementary members
The group password hash for each user
hints: It records users who are supplementary members of the group.
os-users-groups-320.explanation: An `/etc/group` record is group name, password field, GID, and supplementary member list.

os-users-groups-321.title: Primary Group Location
os-users-groups-321.instructions: Where is a user’s primary group ID recorded?
options: Only in the fourth field of `/etc/group`
In the user’s home directory name
hints: The primary GID is one of the seven passwd fields.
os-users-groups-321.explanation: The primary GID is recorded in `/etc/passwd`; the `/etc/group` member list contains supplementary memberships.

os-users-groups-322.title: System and Regular UID Ranges
os-users-groups-322.instructions: Which statement about Linux account ID ranges is correct?
options: Root uses UID 0, system accounts are generally below 1000, and regular users start at 1000
Root uses UID 1000 and all system accounts are above 5000
Regular users must have UIDs below 100
hints: The superuser has a special fixed UID.
os-users-groups-322.explanation: Root uses UID 0; the account ranges described for the system place service accounts below 1000 and regular users from 1000 upward.

os-users-groups-323.title: Create a User with a Home Directory
os-users-groups-323.instructions: Write a command to create user `alice` and create the user’s home directory.
hints: Use the option that creates the home directory.
os-users-groups-323.explanation: `useradd -m alice` creates the account and its home directory.

os-users-groups-324.title: Set a User Login Shell
os-users-groups-324.instructions: Write a command to set user `alice`’s login shell to `/bin/bash`.
hints: Modify the account and specify its shell.
os-users-groups-324.explanation: `usermod -s` changes the login shell for an existing user.

os-users-groups-325.title: Add a User to a Primary Group
os-users-groups-325.instructions: Write a command to change `alice`’s primary group to `engineers`.
hints: Use the lowercase group option for the primary group.
os-users-groups-325.explanation: `usermod -g engineers alice` assigns `engineers` as the primary group.

os-users-groups-326.title: Add Supplementary Groups Safely
os-users-groups-326.instructions: Write a command to add `alice` to supplementary groups `devteam` and `ops` without removing her existing supplementary memberships.
hints: The append flag must be combined with the supplementary-group flag.
os-users-groups-326.explanation: `usermod -aG` appends supplementary group membership; omitting `-a` can replace existing supplementary groups.

os-users-groups-327.title: Create a Group with a GID
os-users-groups-327.instructions: Write a command to create group `engineers` with the explicitly assigned GID `4000`.
hints: Use the group-add command with its numeric-ID option.
os-users-groups-327.explanation: `groupadd -g 4000 engineers` creates the group with GID 4000.

os-users-groups-328.title: Create a System Group
os-users-groups-328.instructions: Write a command to create a system group named `infra`.
hints: The option marks the group as a system group.

os-users-groups-329.title: Rename a Group
os-users-groups-329.instructions: Write a command to rename the existing group `qa` to `quality`.
hints: Use the group-modification command and its name-change option.
os-users-groups-329.explanation: `groupmod -n new_name old_name` renames an existing group.

os-users-groups-330.title: Change a Group GID
os-users-groups-330.instructions: Write a command to change the GID of `devteam` to `3500`.
hints: The group modification command accepts a numeric GID option.
os-users-groups-330.explanation: `groupmod -g 3500 devteam` changes the group’s numeric ID.

os-users-groups-331.title: Switch the Active Primary Group
os-users-groups-331.instructions: A user needs a temporary shell using group `ops` as the primary group. Which command should they run?
hints: This starts a new shell with the selected group active.
os-users-groups-331.explanation: `newgrp ops` starts a new shell with `ops` as the active primary group until that shell ends.

os-users-groups-332.title: Delete a User but Keep Home
os-users-groups-332.instructions: Which command removes user `alice`’s account records while leaving the home directory on disk?
hints: Do not add the recursive home-removal option.
os-users-groups-332.explanation: `userdel alice` removes the account records but leaves the home directory.

os-users-groups-333.title: Delete a User and Home
os-users-groups-333.instructions: Which command removes user `alice` and also removes the home directory and mail spool?
hints: Use the user deletion option that also removes the user’s files.
os-users-groups-333.explanation: `userdel -r alice` removes the account and the home directory/mail spool.

os-users-groups-334.title: Default Account Configuration
os-users-groups-334.instructions: Which file contains default account settings such as UID/GID ranges and the default umask?
hints: It is the system-wide login defaults file.
os-users-groups-334.explanation: `/etc/login.defs` stores defaults used by account-management tools.

os-users-groups-335.title: Prevent Interactive Service Login
os-users-groups-335.instructions: Which login shell can be assigned to a service account to prevent normal interactive logins?
hints: It is a non-login shell path.
os-users-groups-335.explanation: `/sbin/nologin` prevents an account from opening a normal interactive login shell.

os-users-groups-336.title: Password Status
os-users-groups-336.instructions: Write the command to display the password status of user `dev1`.
os-users-groups-336.explanation: `passwd -S` reports account password status, including a locked status indicator.

os-users-groups-337.title: Password Aging Policy
os-users-groups-337.instructions: A user must change a password every 45 days, cannot change it more than once per day, and must receive a warning 7 days before expiry. Write the command for user `qaeng`.
hints: Use maximum age, minimum age, and warning options together.
os-users-groups-337.explanation: `-M 45` sets maximum age, `-m 1` sets minimum age, and `-W 7` sets the warning period.

os-users-groups-338.title: Password Aging Field Meaning
os-users-groups-338.instructions: In a `chage` policy, what does the `-W` option set?
options: The warning period before password expiry
The minimum number of days before a password change
hints: The letter refers to a warning.
os-users-groups-338.explanation: `chage -W` sets the number of days before password expiry when the user is warned.

os-users-groups-339.title: Unlock a User Account
os-users-groups-339.instructions: Write the command to unlock the password for user `tempuser`.

os-users-groups-340.title: Sudo Rule Group Prefix
os-users-groups-340.instructions: In a sudoers rule, what does a leading percent sign in `%wheel` identify?
hints: The symbol distinguishes a group from a single user.
os-users-groups-340.explanation: A leading `%` in sudoers identifies a group.

os-users-groups-341.title: One Elevated Command
os-users-groups-341.instructions: An administrator needs to run only one command with elevated privileges while remaining logged in as their own account. Which command form is intended for this?
hints: Use the command that elevates a specified command rather than opening a full login shell.
os-users-groups-341.explanation: `sudo command` runs a specific command with the privileges permitted by the sudoers policy.

os-shell-syntax-342.title: Search Command History Interactively
os-shell-syntax-342.instructions: You remember part of a long command but not its history number. Which Bash shortcut searches command history interactively?
hints: Hold Control and press the key used for reverse search.
os-shell-syntax-342.explanation: `Ctrl+r` starts an interactive reverse search through Bash history.

os-shell-syntax-343.title: Tab Completion
os-shell-syntax-343.instructions: You have typed the first few characters of an existing command or filename at the Bash prompt. Which key can complete it?
hints: It is the standard shell-completion key.
os-shell-syntax-343.explanation: Pressing Tab requests command or filename completion in Bash.

os-shell-syntax-347.title: Command Substitution
os-shell-syntax-347.instructions: Write a shell expression that prints `Today is ` followed by the output of `date +%F`.
hints: Use `$()` to replace a command expression with its standard output.
os-shell-syntax-347.explanation: `$(date +%F)` is replaced by the command’s output before `echo` runs.

os-shell-syntax-348.title: Escape a Space in a Filename
os-shell-syntax-348.instructions: Write a `touch` command that creates one file named `My File.txt` by escaping the space rather than quoting the name.
hints: A backslash protects the next character from shell interpretation.
os-shell-syntax-348.explanation: The backslash makes the embedded space part of the filename instead of a token separator.

os-shell-syntax-349.title: Brace Expansion versus Globbing
os-shell-syntax-349.instructions: You need to generate the names `report1.txt`, `report2.txt`, and `report3.txt` even if none exists yet. Which shell feature creates those strings before the command runs?
hints: One feature generates a list of strings without checking the filesystem.
os-shell-syntax-349.explanation: Brace expansion generates text such as `report{1..3}.txt`; globbing instead matches existing filenames.

os-environment-350.title: Login Shell Configuration
os-environment-350.instructions: Which per-user Bash file is read for login-shell configuration?

os-environment-351.title: Interactive Non-Login Shell Configuration
os-environment-351.instructions: Which per-user Bash file is commonly read when an interactive non-login Bash shell starts?
hints: It is also the file reloaded by `source` during the exercises.
os-environment-351.explanation: `~/.bashrc` contains interactive Bash configuration such as aliases and environment settings.

os-environment-352.title: Start a Login Bash Shell
os-environment-352.instructions: Write the command that starts a new Bash login shell.
os-environment-352.explanation: `bash --login` starts Bash as a login shell, reading the login configuration.

os-environment-353.title: Remove a Shell Variable
os-environment-353.instructions: Write the command that removes the shell variable `project` from the current shell.
hints: Use the shell built-in for removing a variable.
os-environment-353.explanation: `unset project` removes the variable from the current shell environment.

os-environment-355.title: Alias Expansion Scope
os-environment-355.instructions: An alias works at an interactive prompt but not inside an ordinary shell script. Which statement explains this behavior?
options: Aliases are expanded in interactive shells, not in ordinary scripts
hints: Consider where Bash performs alias expansion.
os-environment-355.explanation: The course material notes that aliases expand in interactive shells and do not normally expand in scripts.

os-environment-356.title: Braced Variable Name
os-environment-356.instructions: A variable named `course` contains `os`. Which expression appends `_linux` to its value without treating `course_linux` as the variable name?
hints: Use braces to mark the variable-name boundary.
os-environment-356.explanation: `${course}_linux` expands the variable `course` and then appends the literal suffix.

os-environment-357.title: Environment Versus Shell Variables
os-environment-357.instructions: Which command displays environment variables inherited by child processes, rather than all shell variables and functions?
hints: The command has the same name as the concept being queried.
os-environment-357.explanation: `env` displays exported environment variables; `set` also includes shell variables and functions.

os-environment-358.title: Find How a Command Is Resolved
os-environment-358.instructions: Write a command to determine how Bash resolves the name `ll` after an alias has been defined.
hints: It can report aliases, built-ins, functions, and executable paths.
os-environment-358.explanation: `type ll` reports how Bash interprets the command name.

os-vim-359.title: Move in Normal Mode
os-vim-359.instructions: Which four keys move the cursor left, down, up, and right in Vim Normal mode, respectively?
hints: They are four adjacent home-row letters.
os-vim-359.explanation: In Normal mode, `h`, `j`, `k`, and `l` move left, down, up, and right.

os-vim-360.title: Delete One Character
os-vim-360.instructions: In Vim Normal mode, which key deletes the character under the cursor?
hints: It is a single key used for character deletion.
os-vim-360.explanation: `x` deletes the character under the cursor in Normal mode.

os-vim-361.title: Insert at Start of Line
os-vim-361.instructions: Which Vim Normal mode key enters Insert mode at the beginning of the current line?
hints: It is the uppercase form of the insert-before-cursor key.
os-vim-361.explanation: `I` enters Insert mode at the beginning of the current line.

os-vim-362.title: Append at End of Line
os-vim-362.instructions: Which Vim Normal mode key enters Insert mode at the end of the current line?
hints: It is the uppercase append command.
os-vim-362.explanation: `A` enters Insert mode at the end of the current line.

os-vim-363.title: Open a Line Above
os-vim-363.instructions: Which Vim Normal mode key opens a new line above the current line and enters Insert mode?
hints: It is the uppercase counterpart of opening a line below.
os-vim-363.explanation: `O` opens a new line above the cursor and enters Insert mode.

os-vim-364.title: Visual Character Selection
os-vim-364.instructions: Which key starts character-wise Visual mode in Vim?

os-vim-365.title: Visual Line Selection
os-vim-365.instructions: Which key starts line-wise Visual mode in Vim?

os-vim-366.title: Visual Block Selection
os-vim-366.instructions: Which Vim shortcut starts block/column Visual mode?
hints: It uses Control with the Visual-mode key.

os-vim-367.title: Copy Three Lines
os-vim-367.instructions: Write the Vim Normal mode command that yanks (copies) the current line and the next two lines.
hints: Put the count before the line-yank command.
os-vim-367.explanation: `3yy` yanks three lines beginning with the current line.

os-vim-368.title: Paste Before the Cursor
os-vim-368.instructions: Which Vim Normal mode key puts yanked or deleted text before the cursor line?
hints: It is the uppercase paste key.
os-vim-368.explanation: `P` puts the text before the cursor; lowercase `p` puts it after/below.

os-vim-369.title: Continue Search
os-vim-369.instructions: After searching forward in Vim with `/term`, which key moves to the next matching occurrence?
os-vim-369.explanation: `n` moves to the next match for the most recent search.

os-vim-370.title: Save As a Different Name
os-vim-370.instructions: Write the Vim command-line mode command to save the current buffer as `newfile.txt` without closing Vim.
hints: Use the write command followed by the destination filename.
os-vim-370.explanation: `:w newfile.txt` writes the current buffer to a file with that name.

os-vim-371.title: Quit Without Changes
os-vim-371.instructions: Which Vim command quits when there are no unsaved changes?
hints: It is the ordinary quit command, without a force marker.
os-vim-371.explanation: `:q` exits Vim when there are no unsaved changes.

os-permissions-372.title: Read Permission on a Directory
os-permissions-372.instructions: A user has read permission on a directory but no execute permission. What can they generally do?
options: List directory entry names but not traverse into them
Modify every file in the directory
Execute every program in the directory
hints: Directory read and execute have different roles.
os-permissions-372.explanation: Read permission allows listing names; execute permission is needed to traverse/search the directory.

os-permissions-373.title: Write and Execute on a Directory
os-permissions-373.instructions: Why does deleting a file normally depend on write and execute permission on its parent directory?
options: Deletion changes the directory entry, and execute permits access to the directory
The file must always be executable
The file must be owned by root
The parent directory must be read-only
hints: Removing a file changes the directory’s list of names.
os-permissions-373.explanation: Write permission allows changing directory entries; execute permission allows accessing/traversing the directory.

os-permissions-374.title: Create Files in a Shared SGID Directory
os-permissions-374.instructions: A team directory has group `projectteam` and mode `2775`. What group ownership should newly created files normally inherit?
hints: The set-group-ID bit on a directory affects new entries.
os-permissions-374.explanation: With SGID set on a directory, new files and subdirectories inherit the directory’s group.

os-permissions-375.title: Recognize SGID in a Listing
os-permissions-375.instructions: A directory’s group-execute position is shown as lowercase `s` in `ls -l`. Which special permission does that indicate?
hints: It is the special bit used for shared group directories.
os-permissions-375.explanation: A lowercase `s` in the group-execute position indicates SGID is set and group execute is enabled.

os-permissions-376.title: Recognize Sticky Bit in a Listing
os-permissions-376.instructions: A shared writable directory ends its permission string with `t`. Which special permission is set?
hints: It restricts deletion in shared directories.
os-permissions-376.explanation: A trailing `t` indicates the sticky bit.

os-permissions-377.title: Sticky Directory Deletion Rule
os-permissions-377.instructions: In a sticky, world-writable directory such as `/tmp`, which users can delete or rename a file?
options: Only the file owner, directory owner, or root
Any user who can read the file
Only members of the file’s group
Any user with read permission on the directory
hints: The sticky bit restricts removal to a small set of owners/administrators.
os-permissions-377.explanation: The sticky bit prevents ordinary users from deleting or renaming files they do not own; the file owner, directory owner, and root can do so.

os-permissions-378.title: SUID on a Shell Script
os-permissions-378.instructions: Does setting SUID on a shell script make it run with the file owner’s effective privileges in the same way as a normal executable?
options: It does not provide the normal SUID behavior for shell scripts
It makes the script run as every group member
It forces the script to run in Vim
It changes the script into a directory
hints: The material distinguishes ordinary executables from shell scripts.
os-permissions-378.explanation: SUID does not provide the normal owner-privilege behavior for shell scripts.

os-permissions-379.title: Set SGID on a Shared Directory
os-permissions-379.instructions: Write a `chmod` command to set mode `2775` on `team_project`.
hints: The leading 2 sets SGID; the remaining digits set rwx permissions.

os-permissions-380.title: Umask 027 for New Files
os-permissions-380.instructions: A shell has umask `0027`. What permissions will a newly created regular file normally receive?
hints: Regular files start from requested mode `0666`.
os-permissions-380.explanation: Applying umask `0027` to the regular-file base mode `0666` leaves `0640` (`rw-r-----`).

os-permissions-381.title: Umask 027 for New Directories
os-permissions-381.instructions: A shell has umask `0027`. What permissions will a newly created directory normally receive?
os-permissions-381.explanation: Applying umask `0027` to the directory base mode `0777` leaves `0750` (`rwxr-x---`).

os-permissions-382.title: Umask 0007 for Shared Files
os-permissions-382.instructions: A collaborative shell uses umask `0007`. What permissions will a newly created regular file normally receive?
hints: Begin with the regular-file base mode `0666`.
os-permissions-382.explanation: Umask `0007` removes all permissions for others, leaving `0660` (`rw-rw----`).

os-permissions-383.title: Display Symbolic Umask
os-permissions-383.instructions: Write the command that displays the current umask in symbolic form.
os-permissions-383.explanation: `umask -S` displays the mask using symbolic permission notation.

os-permissions-384.title: Change Ownership Recursively
os-permissions-384.instructions: Write a command to change the owner to `webadmin` and group to `developers` for `/var/www/html` and everything below it.
hints: Use the recursive option with owner and group separated by a colon.
os-permissions-384.explanation: `chown -R owner:group path` applies ownership changes recursively.

os-permissions-385.title: Who Can Change a File Owner
os-permissions-385.instructions: Which user normally has permission to change a file’s owner to another user?
options: Any user who can read the file
Only a member of the file’s group
hints: Changing ownership is a privileged operation.
os-permissions-385.explanation: Changing a file’s owner requires root privileges in the course’s permission model.

os-find-386.title: Find Symbolic Links
os-find-386.instructions: Write a command to find symbolic links below the current directory.
hints: The file-type code for symbolic links is a lowercase letter.
os-find-386.explanation: `find . -type l` selects symbolic links recursively below the current directory.

os-find-387.title: Find by Group Ownership
os-find-387.instructions: Write a command to find files below `/home` that belong to group `projectteam`.
os-find-387.explanation: `find -group` selects filesystem objects owned by the specified group.

os-find-388.title: Find Unowned Files
os-find-388.instructions: Which `find` predicate selects files whose user account no longer exists?
hints: It identifies objects without a matching user account.
os-find-388.explanation: `-nouser` matches files whose numeric owner has no corresponding user account.

os-find-389.title: Find Files by Access Time
os-find-389.instructions: Write a command to find files under `/home` that were accessed less than five minutes ago.
hints: Access time uses the letter `a`; `-5` means less than five.
os-find-389.explanation: `-amin -5` matches objects accessed less than five minutes ago.

os-find-390.title: Find Files by Status-Change Time
os-find-390.instructions: Write a command to find files under `/home` whose metadata/status changed less than ten minutes ago.
os-find-390.explanation: `-cmin -10` selects objects whose status-change time is less than ten minutes ago.

os-find-391.title: Delete Matching Files with Find
os-find-391.instructions: Write a command to delete files named `*.torrent` below your home directory using `find`’s own delete action.
hints: Use the native delete action after the name test.
os-find-391.explanation: `-delete` removes each matching filesystem entry; verify the search criteria before using it.

os-find-392.title: Execute a Command on Each Match
os-find-392.instructions: Write a command to move every file larger than 10 MiB found under your home directory to `~/Desktop` using `find -exec`.
hints: `{}` is replaced by each match and `\;` ends the action.
os-find-392.explanation: `find -exec` runs the given command for each match; `{}` represents the current path and `\;` terminates the action.

os-archives-393.title: Tar Does Not Compress by Default
os-archives-393.instructions: You create `backup.tar` with `tar -cf`. What does the resulting archive do by itself?
options: Bundles files into one archive without compressing them
hints: Archiving and compression are separate operations.
os-archives-393.explanation: `tar` bundles files and directories; compression is requested separately with an option such as `-z`, `-j`, or `-J`.

os-archives-394.title: Tar Preserves Metadata
os-archives-394.instructions: Why is a tar archive useful for backups compared with simply concatenating file contents?
options: It can preserve ownership, permissions, timestamps, and directory structure
It converts every file to plain text
hints: A backup needs more than the raw contents of files.
os-archives-394.explanation: The archive preserves filesystem metadata such as ownership, permissions, timestamps, and directory structure.

os-archives-395.title: Inspect an Archive Before Extraction
os-archives-395.instructions: Write a command to list the contents of `backup.tar.gz` verbosely without extracting it.
hints: Use the list operation and verbose output.
os-archives-395.explanation: `tar -tvf` lists archive contents in detail without extracting them.

os-archives-396.title: Extract a Tarball to a Destination
os-archives-396.instructions: Write a command to extract `backup.tar.gz` into `/tmp/restore`.
os-archives-396.explanation: `-C /tmp/restore` makes tar extract into that directory; modern tar detects gzip during extraction.

os-archives-397.title: Tar Absolute-Path Safety
os-archives-397.instructions: Why does tar normally remove a leading slash from absolute paths stored in an archive?
options: To avoid overwriting absolute system paths when extracting
To convert symbolic links to hard links
To set every file to mode 777
hints: Think about what happens if an archive is extracted as root.
os-archives-397.explanation: Removing the leading slash makes paths extract relative to the current directory, reducing the risk of overwriting system files.

os-archives-398.title: Dangerous Tar Absolute-Names Option
os-archives-398.instructions: Which tar option preserves absolute pathnames instead of stripping the leading slash?
os-archives-398.explanation: `-P` preserves absolute pathnames and can be dangerous when extracting untrusted archives.

os-archives-399.title: Secure Copy Uses SSH
os-archives-399.instructions: Why can `scp` transfer files to a server that already accepts SSH logins without configuring a separate FTP service?
options: SCP uses the SSH connection and its authentication/security mechanisms
SCP uses the web server’s port 80
hints: The protocol name includes “secure” and shares the remote-shell transport.
os-archives-399.explanation: `scp` uses SSH encryption, host verification, and user authentication.

os-archives-400.title: Rsync Versus SCP for Updates
os-archives-400.instructions: You repeatedly synchronize a large directory and only a small part changes each time. Which tool is described as transferring only modified data blocks?
hints: It is mentioned as an efficient synchronization tool over SSH.
os-archives-400.explanation: `rsync` transfers only modified delta blocks, making repeated updates more efficient than copying everything again.

os-shell-scripts-401.title: Shebang Line
os-shell-scripts-401.instructions: A Bash script must identify the interpreter that should run it. What line should appear first in the script?
hints: It begins with the interpreter directive marker.
os-shell-scripts-401.explanation: `#!/bin/bash` is the shebang that selects Bash as the script interpreter.

os-shell-scripts-402.title: Make a Script Executable
os-shell-scripts-402.instructions: Write the command that adds execute permission to `hello.sh` for all users according to the exercise workflow.
hints: Use the symbolic execute permission with the file-mode command.
os-shell-scripts-402.explanation: `chmod +x` adds execute permission so the script can be run as an executable file.

os-users-groups-403.title: Create a Group with Automatically Assigned GID
os-users-groups-403.instructions: Write a command to create a local group named `ops` without specifying its GID.
hints: Do not provide the numeric-ID option.
os-users-groups-403.explanation: `groupadd ops` creates the group and lets the system assign its GID.

os-users-groups-404.title: Delete a Group
os-users-groups-404.instructions: Write a command to delete the local group named `quality`.
hints: Use the group account deletion utility.

os-users-groups-405.title: Add a Supplementary Group to a User
os-users-groups-405.instructions: Which `usermod` option adds supplementary group membership while preserving the user’s existing supplementary groups?
hints: The append option must be combined with the supplementary-group option.
os-users-groups-405.explanation: `-aG` appends the listed supplementary groups instead of replacing the existing list.

os-users-groups-406.title: Primary Group versus Supplementary Group
os-users-groups-406.instructions: A user belongs to one primary group and several supplementary groups. Which statement is correct?
options: The primary GID is recorded in the user record; supplementary memberships are listed in group records
The primary group is stored only in the home-directory name
A user may have no primary group but must have five supplementary groups
hints: Compare the GID field in the user record with the member list in a group record.
os-users-groups-406.explanation: The user’s primary GID is in `/etc/passwd`; supplementary memberships appear in `/etc/group` member lists.

os-users-groups-407.title: User Private Group
os-users-groups-407.instructions: A newly created regular user is assigned a private group with the same name as the account. What is this arrangement called?
os-users-groups-407.explanation: The user-private-group model creates a matching primary group for an account.

os-shell-syntax-408.title: Root and Regular User Prompts
os-shell-syntax-408.instructions: Which character commonly ends the Bash prompt when the current shell is running as the root superuser?
hints: The regular-user prompt uses a different single character.
os-shell-syntax-408.explanation: A root Bash prompt commonly ends in `#`; a regular user prompt commonly ends in `$`.

os-shell-syntax-409.title: Regular User Prompt
os-shell-syntax-409.instructions: Which character commonly ends the Bash prompt for a regular, non-root user?
hints: The root prompt uses the hash character instead.
os-shell-syntax-409.explanation: A regular-user Bash prompt commonly ends in `$`; a root prompt commonly ends in `#`.

os-shell-syntax-410.title: Single Quotes Suppress Expansion
os-shell-syntax-410.instructions: You need the literal text `$HOME` to appear without expanding the variable. Which quoting style should you use?
hints: This quoting style preserves every character inside it literally.
os-shell-syntax-410.explanation: Single quotes suppress variable and command expansion inside the quoted text.

os-shell-syntax-411.title: Double Quotes Preserve Spaces and Allow Variables
os-shell-syntax-411.instructions: A variable named `name` should expand inside a greeting, and the greeting should remain one argument even if the value contains spaces. Which command form does this?
hints: Use the quoting style that permits variable expansion but protects spaces.
os-shell-syntax-411.explanation: Double quotes allow `$name` to expand while keeping the resulting text together as one shell word.

os-file-inspection-412.title: File Extension Does Not Determine Type
os-file-inspection-412.instructions: A file named `image.txt` contains binary image data. Which statement about its type is correct on Linux?
options: The extension alone determines the type
The `file` command can identify the type from its contents
The shell treats every `.txt` file as plain text
hints: Linux commonly inspects file contents rather than trusting the suffix.
os-file-inspection-412.explanation: Filename extensions do not define a file’s actual type; `file` inspects content characteristics.

os-file-inspection-413.title: View a File One Line at a Time
os-file-inspection-413.instructions: When using `more` to view a long file, which key advances the display by one line?
hints: It is the key used to submit a command at a prompt.
os-file-inspection-413.explanation: In `more`, Space advances by a page and Enter advances by one line.

os-redirection-414.title: Standard Input File Descriptor
os-redirection-414.instructions: What numeric file descriptor represents standard input?
hints: It is the first of the three standard streams.
os-redirection-414.explanation: Standard input is file descriptor 0; standard output is 1 and standard error is 2.

os-redirection-415.title: Standard Output File Descriptor
os-redirection-415.instructions: What numeric file descriptor represents standard output?
hints: It is the stream used for normal command output.

os-redirection-416.title: Append Standard Error
os-redirection-416.instructions: Write the redirection operator that appends a command’s standard-error output to an existing file rather than overwriting it.
hints: Use the file descriptor for errors followed by the append operator.
os-redirection-416.explanation: `2>>` appends standard-error output to the specified file.

os-redirection-417.title: Redirect Both Output Streams
os-redirection-417.instructions: Write the Bash redirection operator that sends both standard output and standard error to the same file.
hints: It combines an ampersand with the overwrite operator.
os-redirection-417.explanation: `&>` redirects both standard output and standard error in Bash.

os-find-418.title: Find Recently Modified Files
os-find-418.instructions: Write a command to find items under `/home` modified less than ten minutes ago.
hints: Modification time in minutes uses the letter `m`.
os-find-418.explanation: `-mmin -10` matches items modified less than ten minutes ago.

os-find-419.title: Find Files with a Specific User Owner
os-find-419.instructions: Write a command to find files under `/home` owned by user `andrew`.
hints: Use the owner predicate, not the group predicate.
os-find-419.explanation: `-user andrew` selects objects owned by that user.

os-find-420.title: Find Objects with Missing User Account
os-find-420.instructions: Which `find` predicate identifies filesystem objects whose numeric owner has no matching user account?
hints: The predicate name states that the user record is absent.
os-find-420.explanation: `-nouser` finds filesystem objects whose owner ID does not map to a user account.

os-find-421.title: Find Files by Size Range
os-find-421.instructions: Write a command to find files under `/usr/bin` larger than 2 MiB and smaller than 10 MiB.
hints: Combine a greater-than and a less-than size test.
os-find-421.explanation: The two `-size` predicates restrict results to the requested size interval.

os-archives-422.title: Create a Gzip Archive Verbosely
os-archives-422.instructions: Write a `tar` command to create `backup.tar.gz` from `project/`, showing the files as they are added.
hints: Combine create, gzip, verbose, and filename options.
os-archives-422.explanation: `-c` creates, `-z` uses gzip, `-v` lists processed files, and `-f` names the archive.

os-archives-423.title: Create an XZ-Compressed Archive
os-archives-423.instructions: Which `tar` command creates an xz-compressed archive named `backup.tar.xz` from `project/`?
hints: The xz option uses an uppercase letter.
os-archives-423.explanation: `tar -cJf` creates an archive using xz compression.

os-archives-424.title: Copy a Directory to a Remote Server
os-archives-424.instructions: Write an `scp` command to copy the local directory `reports/` recursively to `/home/alice/` on `alice@server.example`.
hints: Use the recursive option and the `user@host:path` form.
os-archives-424.explanation: `scp -r` copies a directory tree over SSH.

os-archives-425.title: Use a Custom SSH Port with SCP
os-archives-425.instructions: Write an `scp` command to copy `report.txt` to `alice@server.example:/home/alice/` using SSH port `2222`.
hints: The scp port option is uppercase.
os-archives-425.explanation: `scp -P` specifies the SSH port used for the transfer.

os-networking-500.title: Recognize a Local IPv4 Address
os-networking-500.instructions: Which address is in one of the local-network IPv4 ranges identified in the course?
hints: The course uses the `192.168.x.x` and `10.x.x.x` ranges as local-network examples.
os-networking-500.explanation: `192.168.x.x` is a local-network IPv4 range; `127.0.0.1` is the loopback address.

os-networking-501.title: IP Address and Port
os-networking-501.instructions: A client must contact the web service on a remote machine. Which pair identifies the destination described in the networking lesson?
options: The server IP address and the web-service port
The user name and shell name
The DNS resolver and the local home directory
hints: The server address identifies the computer; the port identifies the service.
os-networking-501.explanation: The client connects to a server IP address at a particular port to reach a service.

os-shell-syntax-502.title: Use set to Inspect Shell State
os-shell-syntax-502.instructions: Which Bash built-in displays shell variables and functions, including values that are not exported to child processes?
hints: It displays more than the exported environment.
os-shell-syntax-502.explanation: `set` displays shell variables and functions; `env` displays exported environment variables.

os-shell-scripts-503.title: Run a Script Found through PATH
os-shell-scripts-503.instructions: After adding the personal `bin` directory to `PATH`, write the command used to run the executable script `hello.sh` from that directory.
hints: Use a dot followed by a slash to refer to the current directory.
os-shell-scripts-503.explanation: Once its directory is on `PATH`, the executable script can be started by its command name, `hello.sh`.

os-permissions-504.title: Strict Umask Profile
os-permissions-504.instructions: A shell uses umask `0077`. What permissions will a newly created regular file normally receive?
hints: Regular files start from requested mode `0666`.
os-permissions-504.explanation: Applying umask `0077` to `0666` leaves `0600`, so only the owner can read and write the new file.

os-permissions-505.title: Uppercase S in a Permission Listing
os-permissions-505.instructions: In the owner-execute position of an `ls -l` permission string, what does an uppercase `S` indicate?
options: SUID is set but the owner-execute permission is not
SGID is set and group execute is enabled
The file is a symbolic link
hints: It is the SUID marker when the ordinary execute bit is absent.
os-permissions-505.explanation: Uppercase `S` in the owner-execute position means SUID is set while owner execute is not set.

os-find-506.title: Find by Metadata Change Time
os-find-506.instructions: Write a command to find items under `/home` whose metadata changed less than ten minutes ago.
hints: Status-change time uses `c` and the minute suffix.
os-find-506.explanation: `-cmin -10` selects items whose metadata/status changed within the last ten minutes.

os-users-groups-507.title: Set the Default Editor Environment Variable
os-users-groups-507.instructions: Write a shell command that exports `EDITOR` with the value `vim` to child processes.
os-users-groups-507.explanation: `export EDITOR=vim` makes the variable part of the environment inherited by child processes.
